findings.title: Findings converge on the SessionStart embedding backfill spawn (D5)
findings.why_it_matters: The mechanism is D5's second detached process: `ccrecall backfill embeddings`, spawned by `ccrecall-setup` at each session start under a 4096-token cap. Six findings land on it from different sides: what it selects (Finding 4), what happens when it gets killed (Finding 5), how its queue stalls (Finding 6), how the hook decides to start it (Finding 7), how it collides with other writers (Finding 8), and an alert that tells users to run the manual command it was meant to replace (Finding 11). D5's table prices it as "a spawn, a cap flag, a batch size". The local fixes add a policy reversal, a breadcrumb, a memory check, a setting, a watermark rule change, a hook predicate, an ordering rule and an alert rewrite. Does this point to a structural problem with the mechanism that should be re-evaluated, rather than fixed finding by finding? Re-evaluation is open-ended: it includes whether the mechanism is needed at all, and whether some failure modes are limitations to accept and document. The goal of no manual command is not what is in question, only whether this is the mechanism that delivers it. The convergence test is met by at least one change: starting the run at the end of the import child rather than from a second hook spawn would remove Finding 7's hook predicate and the D3/D5 ordering rule in Finding 8. That example shows the findings share a cause. It is not a proposal.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the SessionStart embedding backfill spawn before addressing Findings 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 11 individually. Open questions: What should trigger the run? Which branches may it select? What stops it from repeating after a kill? How does it behave while other writers run? What should the draft alert say? Is the mechanism needed at all, and which failure modes are limitations to accept?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the SessionStart embedding backfill spawn before addressing Findings 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 11 individually. Open questions: What should trigger the run? Which branches may it select? What stops it from repeating after a kill? How does it behave while other writers run? What should the draft alert say? Is the mechanism needed at all, and which failure modes are limitations to accept?
findings.choice_reason: embedding backfill can stay manual; a manual invocation that fixes old records is fine

findings.title: The spawned child denies itself the PID lock, so repair and the D5 backfill never run
findings.why_it_matters: D3 says "no new machinery; the spawned import turns repair on". That does not work with the current PID handling. `_spawn_background` creates the marker and writes the child's PID into it. A child running with `--repair-gaps` calls `try_acquire_pid_file`, finds a live PID in the marker (its own), and returns False. It then skips the whole run with exit 0, including the ordinary import loop, because the guard sits at the top of `_run`. So turning on the flag doesn't only leave repair inert: it also stops the background import that runs today. D5's child has the same shape: `cmd_backfill_embeddings` acquires the same kind of guard and exits `EXIT_OK`. Tests that call `run(repair_gaps=True)` directly would pass while every field run skips.
findings.recommended: B: `try_acquire_pid_file` treats a marker holding `os.getpid()` as already acquired. Add a test that goes through `_spawn_background` end to end and asserts the work happened.
findings.chosen: B: `try_acquire_pid_file` treats a marker holding `os.getpid()` as already acquired. Add a test that goes through `_spawn_background` end to end and asserts the work happened.

findings.title: The background path never writes the ok cache, so every import re-parses every transcript
findings.why_it_matters: D3 prices steady state at "up to a few seconds", from a warm `status --check-ingestion`. Only `summarize_ingestion` writes `ingestion_check_cache`. `classify_sessions` and `find_repairable_sessions` yield "ok" without recording it. The walk-version token invalidates all 10,075 rows on this machine, and nothing on the background path refills them. Each spawned import then parses every session's transcript again, until the user happens to run `status --check-ingestion`. Measured here on a random read-only sample of 300 sessions: 219 MB in 1.93 CPU seconds, which extrapolates to about 69 CPU seconds across 9,931 sessions and 7.82 GB. With at least 282 imports over two days, that is about 2.7 CPU hours a day on this desktop. With a warm cache the same classification took 3.8 s wall over 6,959 sessions, so D3's figure is right only if something keeps the cache warm. Memory looks fine: 68 MB max RSS on the sample, and the largest session is 32.7 MB, not the hundreds of MB one report suggests.
findings.recommended: B: The repair path records ok verdicts in a batch, committed before the first repair candidate. D3's table gets the measured cold and warm numbers.
findings.chosen: B: The repair path records ok verdicts in a batch, committed before the first repair candidate. D3's table gets the measured cold and warm numbers.

findings.title: D5's selection isn't scoped to repaired sessions, so it becomes an unprompted full-history embed
findings.why_it_matters: D5 asks whether "repaired sessions" should get embedded without a manual command, but its selection is `build_selection`: any active branch with a stale or missing watermark, a chunk without a vector, or a draft chunk. Anyone who never ran the opt-in backfill has their entire history in that set, and a future `EMBEDDING_VERSION` bump queues the whole corpus the same way. The code's comments state the opposite policy: full-history embedding "never fires unbidden". D5 reverses that for everyone and describes it only as "a slow drain of large backlogs". At the rate in this machine's nightly logs (19-24 exchanges per about 3m10s, an upper bound since those runs are full cap and mostly long exchanges), a history the size of this one (18,053 chunks) is on the order of tens of CPU hours, spread across session starts.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the full-history selection, restate D5 as a deliberate reversal of the opt-in policy, and update the comments that state the old one.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A branch that gets OOM-killed is retried first at every session start
findings.why_it_matters: The content-error sentinel only protects against Python exceptions, which `_embed_one_branch` catches and marks `embedding_version = -1`. An OOM kill runs no handler, so nothing is marked. Each finished branch commits on RELEASE (confirmed by a probe) and selection is `ORDER BY id`, so the branch that triggered the kill is first in line next time. Each session start respawns the process, it gets killed again, and it can take other work on the host with it. The stale marker is reaped by liveness, so nothing breaks the loop. D5 itself says supported installs have far less free memory than the 4 GB peak, and this path has killed WSL before. There is no off switch: D5's Reversibility is removing the spawn, which is a code change in the next release. `lower_scheduling_priority` is CPU nice only and does nothing for memory.
findings.recommended: C: Do B and also skip the spawn when available memory is below the known peak.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A capped run stalls behind its own draft branches
findings.why_it_matters: D5 says the automatic run "must not select chunks for draft upgrade", but removing the draft clause doesn't achieve that. `_should_stamp_watermark` withholds the watermark from any branch holding a truncated chunk, so the `embedding_version < ?` clause still matches it. A capped pass over such a branch does no inference (`_diff_exchanges` at target cap 4096 finds nothing to do), stamps nothing, and still returns `updated=1`. `--limit` counts `updated`, so a small limit is used up on the same branches at the head of `ORDER BY id`. Without a limit, the next batch matches the last one and the stuck guard aborts the run. Once the head of the queue holds a limit's worth of truncated branches, the drain makes no progress and reports success. Separately, the capped entry point doesn't exist yet (`cap_limit=MODEL_TOKEN_LIMIT` is hardcoded) and the ledger doesn't give the spawn's argv, so the claimed thread and nice settings hold only if the argv omits `--threads`.
findings.recommended: A: `_should_stamp_watermark` stops treating truncation as "not current". The automatic run drops the draft clause, and the ledger names the capped entry point and the spawn's exact argv.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The D5 spawn needs a check that the hook can't compute from the real selection
findings.why_it_matters: The design doesn't say how `ccrecall-setup` decides to start the backfill. It can't reuse `build_selection`. That function references `chunk_vec`, which only exists with sqlite-vec loaded, and invariant 3 forbids loading it on the hook path. Importing `backfill_query` also pulls `ccrecall.embeddings` and numpy onto the hook. So a hook-side check is a second, narrower definition of "needs embedding". Spawning unconditionally has its own cost: `run()` loads the model before it selects anything, so a start with no work still pays for a model load. The PID key also lives in the heavy module, unlike the other spawn keys in `config.py`.
findings.recommended: A: Drop the hook check. The import child, having finished repair, starts the capped backfill when `build_selection` finds work.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Repair, the backfill and Stop-hook sync contend for the writer lock, and D3 and D5 start together
findings.why_it_matters: The backfill holds SQLite's writer lock across each branch's whole inference, because its pre-delete runs inside the SAVEPOINT before embedding. Sync does the same inside its one transaction. A probe confirms a second writer gets "database is locked" in both shapes. All of these connections use a 30 s busy timeout. At this machine's nightly rate of about 8 s per exchange (full cap, upper bound), a branch of more than a few exchanges can outlast it, and the largest branch here has 82. When it does, a Stop-hook sync logs "Sync error" and leaves the live session unsynced until the next Stop; a repair run hitting `OperationalError` aborts its remaining candidates; and a backfill hitting one exits `EXIT_ABORT`. D3 and D5 as drawn also start in the same `main()`, so the two background jobs contend from their first moment, most heavily on the first run after upgrade. All of this recovers on the next Stop or session start.
findings.recommended: A: Run the backfill after the import finishes, and record in the ledger that Stop-hook syncs may miss during long branches and recover on the next Stop.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Unrepairable sessions are re-parsed and force-reimported on every background import
findings.why_it_matters: A session that stays non-ok after repair is never cached, so each run parses it, force-reimports it, and parses it again to reclassify, with a log line nobody watches. `repair_sessions`'s own docstring says "reattempting won't help". D3 ratified the retry, but the ledger gives no bound on how many sessions are affected. The critics both want a negative cache. That needs more than they describe: `ingestion_check_cache` has no verdict column, so it means a schema change, which D3 chose the walk token to avoid, or a separate store.
findings.recommended: A: Keep the ratified retry, and add the measured count to D3's table. Revisit if the repair log shows a large unrepairable count.
findings.chosen: B: Record non-ok verdicts in a negative cache so a session is retried only when its source changes.

findings.title: Nothing reports when repair isn't working or the backfill keeps dying
findings.why_it_matters: Both spawns are detached with stdout and stderr on DEVNULL. The repair summary is a `print`, so it disappears; only the `log.info` progress lines reach `ccrecall-import.log`. A non-zero exit from failures has no one to read it. The SessionStart alert block has an embedding-status sidecar that records only model and vec unavailability, and no alert for ingestion gaps. An OOM kill, a stuck batch, or the self-skip in Finding 2 produces nothing a user would see. This is a dark operation under `logging.md`: the symptom is "my old sessions still don't show up in search".
findings.recommended: B: Log the summary, and add reason codes to the embedding-status sidecar for a persistently failing repair and for a backfill that died uncleanly, so the existing alert and snooze surface them.
findings.chosen: B: Log the summary, and add reason codes to the embedding-status sidecar for a persistently failing repair and for a backfill that died uncleanly, so the existing alert and snooze surface them.

findings.title: The draft-quality alert tells users to run the command D5 replaces
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: users who rely on SessionStart alerts staying quiet. The alert fires when any active branch has a chunk below 8192 tokens and no schedule marker exists. Its text tells the user to run `ccrecall backfill embeddings`, the ~8.4 GB manual path, or to set up a schedule. D5's automatic run produces exactly those draft chunks, so users who were never told to run anything get told to. The senior engineer couldn't find this code and left it unverified; it is at `hooks/context_alerts.py`, and the trigger is as described.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the SessionStart alert keeps offering the manual full-quality upgrade for draft chunks.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The walk and the summary skip can disagree when a hop crosses files
findings.why_it_matters: `_expected_uuids` merges a session's files, while `sync_session` and the Stop-hook sync see one file. A boundary whose `logicalParentUuid` is in another file resolves in the merged view and dangles in the single-file view. Because D2 makes the summary's presence depend on whether the hop resolves, the two views then disagree about the summary and the earlier chain. The session stays `ingestion_gap`, and a group repair can be undone by the next single-file sync. The design's "indexing and the ingestion check agree" holds only for equal inputs.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hop crossing files can leave that session with a perpetual gap that retries.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a hop crossing files can leave that session with a perpetual gap that retries.

findings.title: A repair can overwrite a resumed session's newest links
findings.why_it_matters: Repair and Stop-hook sync hold different PID keys, so they can act on the same session. `pending_tail` protects only sessions touched in the last 15 minutes. Repair parses before it gets the writer lock, so a stale parse can commit after a sync and have `diff_branch_messages` drop links the sync just added. The report's stated harm, a "current" watermark over missing chunks, isn't reachable as written: each writer's work is one transaction, and D4's clear moves the watermark in the safe direction. What remains is the newest turns being unlinked until the next Stop or repair.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a repair racing a resumed session can briefly unlink its newest turns until the next Stop or repair.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a repair racing a resumed session can briefly unlink its newest turns until the next Stop or repair.

findings.title: An older install sharing the database undoes stitched links
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a public install where an older ccrecall shares ~/.ccrecall with a newer one, e.g. a plugin copy plus a pip copy, or a rollback. D3 chose a walk token over a schema bump so that older installs aren't warned. An older install's Stop hook still walks one chain, and `diff_branch_messages` removes every link outside it, so it un-stitches any compacted session it syncs. The newer install repairs it again. The cache half is narrower than reported: an older install writes cache rows only through its own `status --check-ingestion`, so ordinary hook activity doesn't flip the whole cache.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: with two versions on one database, the older one's syncs undo stitching for the sessions it touches until the newer one repairs them.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: with two versions on one database, the older one's syncs undo stitching for the sessions it touches until the newer one repairs them.

findings.title: The spawn is conditional, so "always repairs gaps" never fires on existing installs
"No higher peak than ccrecall already runs unprompted" is false once the backfill overlaps a sync
Findings converge on D3's non-ok verdicts in `ingestion_check_cache`
findings.why_it_matters: The mechanism is D3's negative cache: a verdict column on `ingestion_check_cache`, so a session that repair can't fix isn't retried until its source or the walk changes. Both critics land on it from different sides: when the verdict is written (Finding 2), which outcomes may be written (Finding 3), where it is read (Finding 4), what expires or overrides it (Finding 5), and how the column gets added (Finding 6). Each local fix adds a rule to the mechanism. D3 was ratified with the schema bump's cost on the table, and these five were not. Does this point to a structural problem with the mechanism that should be re-evaluated, rather than fixed finding by finding? Re-evaluation is open-ended: it includes whether the mechanism is needed at all, and whether some failure modes are limitations to accept. The convergence test is met by at least one change: without non-ok verdicts, none of Findings 2-6 needs a fix, because ok verdicts already have one writer pattern and one meaning. That example shows the findings share a cause. It is not a proposal. Evidence on the other side: spec 016 said a persisted marker was out of scope "unless `--repair-gaps` moves to automated/repeated invocation", which is what D3 does, and the operational-resilience critic holds that the fault is how the cache is written, not that it exists.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate non-ok verdicts before addressing Findings 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 individually. Open questions: Are they needed, given the measured retry cost? Who writes one and who reads it? Which outcomes count? What expires or overrides one? Where do they live?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate non-ok verdicts before addressing Findings 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 individually. Open questions: Are they needed, given the measured retry cost? Who writes one and who reads it? Which outcomes count? What expires or overrides one? Where do they live?
findings.choice_reason: re-evaluation dropped the negative cache: retry every import

findings.title: D3 doesn't place the non-ok write, and both obvious placements break something
findings.why_it_matters: D3 says "the batch commits before the first repair candidate" and "non-ok verdicts are recorded too". Read literally, every candidate gets a non-ok verdict before anything has tried to repair it. If the run then stops (a `sqlite3.OperationalError` re-raise, a kill, WSL shutdown), the candidates it never reached hit the cached verdict on the next import and are skipped as known-unrepairable, with no error anywhere. The other placement, writing inside the loop after `reclassify_session`, has its own failure. It is a plain `INSERT OR REPLACE` on a connection in Python's default transaction mode, which opens a transaction before DML but not before `SAVEPOINT`. Every later candidate's `SAVEPOINT` then nests in that transaction and its `RELEASE` commits nothing, so the per-candidate durability in the module docstring is gone. A probe reproduces this: after one in-loop write, `in_transaction` stays True through the next candidate's RELEASE, and closing without a commit loses that candidate. The operational-resilience report's fix ("in the same commit as that candidate's SAVEPOINT release") needs a further change, because `reclassify_session` runs after the RELEASE.
findings.recommended: A: Ok verdicts go before the loop. A non-ok verdict is written after the candidate's `reclassify_session` and committed immediately, with a test that a later candidate's `conn.in_transaction` is False at its SAVEPOINT and that a run stopped midway leaves unreached candidates repairable.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Which outcomes may be cached as non-ok is unspecified, and some aren't facts about the session
findings.why_it_matters: The cache key is a source fingerprint plus a DB-coverage fingerprint. D3 says "non-ok verdicts are recorded" without naming categories, and not all of them are functions of those inputs. `pending_tail` versus `stale_tail` depends on the clock: a cached `pending_tail` replays forever for an unchanged source, so a session that has since become `stale_tail` is never offered for repair. `missing_source` is a stat-time race. A candidate that failed with a poison exception is an operational failure. `repair_sessions` also counts `pending_tail` and `missing_source` results as `sessions_unrepairable`, so "unrepairable" alone isn't a safe filter.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A cached non-ok hit makes `status --check-ingestion` under-report, and `_cached_ok_fingerprint` would read it as ok
findings.why_it_matters: If the verdict is consulted where the ok cache is, inside `classify_sessions`, a hit returns `missing_indices = []`. `summarize_ingestion` adds `len(missing_indices)` to `*_turns`, so the status report shows gap sessions with 0 missing turns, for exactly the sessions that are still broken. The ledger's last Assumed bullet relies on that diagnostic. Two more consumers sit on the same path. `reclassify_session`'s docstring relies on the cache missing after a repair, and after a no-op repair the fingerprints are unchanged, so it would replay the old verdict. And `_cached_ok_fingerprint` compares fingerprints only: unless it also filters on the new column, line 190 yields "ok" for a non-ok row, which would hide the session entirely.
findings.recommended: A: `find_repairable_sessions` drops sessions with a matching non-ok verdict from `sources` before classifying. `classify_sessions` keeps an ok-only short-circuit, with `_cached_ok_fingerprint` filtering on the verdict.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: A negative verdict can outlive what it describes, and nothing forces a retry
findings.why_it_matters: A verdict depends on `_entry_expects_message`, `message_content_parts` and the insert path as well as the walk, but only source changes, DB changes and the walk token invalidate it. A later release that fixes one of those leaves already-cached sessions suppressed on every install, with nothing telling anyone. Today `ccrecall import --repair-gaps` retries every candidate, so it is the user's lever. Once `find_repairable_sessions` skips cached sessions, it silently does nothing for them. The data-integrity report calls the fix two one-liners, with explicit CLI runs ignoring verdicts and only the spawned run honoring them. That isn't quite right: D3's spawn turns repair on by adding the same flag to `["ccrecall", "import"]`, so the CLI can't tell the two apart without a second flag.
findings.recommended: B: Do A, and have the spawn pass an internal flag that honors verdicts, so an explicit `ccrecall import --repair-gaps` keeps retrying every candidate.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: `_migrate_to_v10` has two placements that fail
findings.why_it_matters: `SCHEMA_CORE` creates `ingestion_check_cache` on every open, before migrations. Adding the column there and in an `ALTER` gives "duplicate column name" on a fresh install unless the v6-style guard is present. Adding it only in the version-gated block means a database already ahead of this code returns early from `_apply_migrations` at the `current >= SCHEMA_VERSION` check and never gets the column, so this install's verdict INSERT fails with "no such column". The ledger says only "gains a verdict column in `_migrate_to_v10`".
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The repair alert doesn't fit the single-slot embedding sidecar
findings.why_it_matters: D3 reports a failing repair with a new reason code in the embedding-status sidecar, and tells `clear_embedding_failure` callers to scope their clears. You ratified that in round 1 over a dedicated sidecar, on the expectation that it reused what exists. Reading the code, scoping fixes one of five problems. The sidecar holds one `{reason, since}` record that `record_embedding_failure` replaces whole, so a repair reason can erase a live `model_unavailable` record and the reverse. Backfill's success path clears unconditionally by design, and D5 makes that a manual run, so a successful backfill erases an unrelated repair alert. The alert's intro and action are fixed to `ALERT_EMBEDDINGS_FAILING`: a repair failure would announce "embedding pipeline is failing" and advise verifying sqlite-vec. Snooze is per alert key, so the two failures suppress each other. And "persistently" has no source: nothing stores a count, and the child sees only its own run, so it collapses to "failed once". The reuse needs a new reason, new prose, a clear rule, a snooze key and a counter, which is the machinery it was meant to avoid.
findings.recommended: B: Add a dedicated repair-status sidecar with its own alert key and prose, recording N consecutive failed runs and resetting on a clean run, including the abort path.
findings.chosen: A: Drop the repair alert. The summary goes to the log, and `status --check-ingestion` remains the check.

findings.title: Stale chunks stay searchable after repair, and the ledger says otherwise
findings.why_it_matters: D4 clears `branches.embedding_version` so backfill picks the branch up, but vector search never reads that watermark. It filters per chunk on `ch.embedding_version`, `ch.embedding_model` and `b.is_active`. So until the next backfill, a repaired session still has its old chunks live in semantic search, including the compact-summary recap D2 removes going forward. Their `exchange_index` values come from the one-chain branch, while the repaired branch numbers the earlier chain first. The text and `first_message_uuid` remain real, so the harm is a duplicate recap and an index that doesn't match, not a wrong result. Two ledger sentences are inaccurate as a result. D5's Ratified says repaired sessions "have keyword search only" (they also have old-chain semantic hits). Posture says repair changes chunks (with `embed=False` it changes none).
findings.recommended: A: Accept as a known limitation: a repaired session keeps its old chunks, including the recap, until the next backfill. Correct the sentences in Posture and D5.
findings.chosen: A: Accept as a known limitation: a repaired session keeps its old chunks, including the recap, until the next backfill. Correct the sentences in Posture and D5.

findings.title: D4's "embedding didn't run" should be read from `vec_writable`, not inferred from a count
findings.why_it_matters: `embed_branch_chunks` returns 0 for three different reasons: embedding skipped, nothing needing embedding, and no embeddable exchange (where it has just stamped the watermark). If the D4 clear infers "didn't run" from that return, it un-stamps a correct watermark and causes a pointless backfill pass on ordinary links-changed syncs. `sync_branch` already holds the answer: it receives `is_active` and `vec_writable`, and the early return is exactly `not (is_active and vec_writable)`. So nothing needs inferring, and no new return status is required. The report's second suggestion, skipping the clear when `vec_writable` is False, must not be applied: `session_ops.py:148` computes `vec_writable = embed and chunk_vec_queryable(conn)`, so every `embed=False` import has it False, and that would disable D4 for the repair path it exists for. The report's "pins every touched branch at 0 forever" on no-vec installs isn't a real harm either: the column defaults to 0 and is stamped only by embedding, so on those installs it was already 0, and 0 is truthful.
findings.chosen: State in D4 that the clear's condition is `links_changed and not (is_active and vec_writable)`, read from `sync_branch`'s own arguments and not from `embed_branch_chunks`'s return value. Add a test that a links-changed sync with embedding enabled and nothing to embed keeps its stamped watermark, and that an `embed=False` import clears it.

findings.title: A verdict batch written at the end of the cold scan loses all progress on a kill
findings.why_it_matters: D3 prices the first run at about 69 CPU seconds of parsing and records verdicts in a batch. Written as one transaction after classification, like the existing `ok_cache_writes` pattern, a kill during the scan saves nothing and the next spawn starts over. The cache is what makes this a one-time cost, so an install that keeps getting interrupted keeps paying it.
findings.chosen: State in D3 that ok verdicts are flushed every few hundred sessions with a commit each, finishing before the first repair candidate, so progress survives a kill and no transaction is open when the repair loop starts. Correct the "pure-SELECT" statement in the `import_repair.py` docstring in the same change.

findings.title: The unified walk has no stated cycle guard, and the copy without one now runs unattended
findings.why_it_matters: D1 merges two walks that differ on this one property. `find_all_branches` keeps a visited set, with a comment saying the transcript is untrusted. `_expected_uuids` has none, and its `ordered_branch` list grows on every pass. D1 doesn't say which behaviour survives, and the hop adds a new way to form a cycle: a boundary whose `logicalParentUuid` names a later entry. A probe on a three-entry cycle confirms the split: `find_all_branches` returns, and `_expected_uuids` was still running when a 10-second timeout killed it (exit 124). After D3 that code runs in the detached SessionStart import, where a hang holds the import PID marker with a live PID, so every later import is skipped, with nothing logged and memory growing.
findings.chosen: State in D1 that the helper keeps `find_all_branches`'s visited set across hops, so a revisit ends the walk, the same outcome as a pointer that doesn't resolve. Add a test with a parent cycle and a hop that points downstream, called through `_expected_uuids`.

findings.title: Counting the caller's own PID as acquired infers ownership wrongly when a PID is recycled
"Unrepairable" is wrongly inferred when a partly repaired session later grows
